title: Pre-warm node pools runbook (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working draft runbook for pre-warming node pools to reduce cold-start latency for inference-serving workloads (especially GPU-backed model servers and stateful KV-caches). The goal is to shorten 95th/99th-percentile request latency during traffic spikes by ensuring a minimum warm capacity is available without over-provisioning constant headroom.

Context / problem statement:
- On sudden traffic spikes when models are invoked (hosted API bursts or batch rollouts), cluster autoscaling + image pulls + node boot time currently add 10s-120s of tail latency depending on instance type and region.
- For latency-sensitive customers we observed failures where the application timed out before node kubelet registration finished and kube-proxy/CNI ready, causing request errors and client retries.
- Cold nodes also miss warm KV cache (prefix/KV), increasing per-token compute cost during the first requests.

When to trigger pre-warm strategy:
- Regular scheduled daily traffic ramps (regional morning peaks)
- Before planned traffic-generating experiments (campaigns, marketing blasts, large customer demos)
- Canary rollouts that change model versions and could create temporary cold-cache pressure
- When alert: cluster_node_provisioning_latency > steady-state baseline for 3m

High-level policy options (pick one per pool):
1) Static warm pool: maintain N spare nodes on a small dedicated node pool (easiest, higher cost).
2) Scheduled warm-up: cron-based scaling to N nodes ahead of expected ramp (cost efficient for predictable events).
3) Reactive pre-warm: short-lived pre-pulls + admission queueing—triggered by forecasted surge signal.
4) Hybrid: scheduled base + reactive burst to target.

Recommended defaults for inference-GPU pools (starting point):
- Minimum spare nodes: 2 x GPU nodes per AZ for production-slo pools (model-serving-critical)
- Warmup window: start 8 minutes before expected ramp for n1-standard-like instances, 12–20 minutes for cold-on-demand GPUs depending on image size and startup scripts.
- Image pull concurrency: ensure nodes use local caching (daemonset pre-pull) and use smaller golden images where possible.

Concrete steps (operational playbook) - quick run:
1) Validate signal
   - Check alert/forecast: Prometheus query examples:
     - cluster_node_provisioning_latency_seconds_bucket{job="cluster-autoscaler"}
     - predict request rate: sum(rate(api_requests_total[1m])) by (route)
   - Confirm event time and blast size.
2) Choose strategy: ad-hoc scheduled vs static warm pool. If this is a one-off (campaign) use scheduled warmup.
3) For scheduled warmup (GKE example)
   - Increase node-pool size: gcloud container clusters resize --cluster=CLUSTER --node-pool=POOL --num-nodes=TARGET --region=REGION
   - For EKS: eksctl scale nodegroup --cluster CLUSTER --name POOL --nodes TARGET
   - For Karpenter: create a nodeTemplate patch or temporarily adjust provisioner constraints to allow extra capacity (replica= +N)
4) Ensure images and startup artifacts are present:
   - Apply a DaemonSet pre-puller to the pool with tolerations/affinity targeting new nodes:
     kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
     apiVersion: apps/v1
     kind: DaemonSet
     metadata:
       name: image-prepull
     spec:
       selector:
         matchLabels:
           name: image-prepull
       template:
         metadata:
           labels:
             name: image-prepull
         spec:
           containers:
           - name: prepull
             image: alpine:3.18
             command: ["/bin/sh","-c","docker pull us-docker-repo/redwood-model-server:gold && sleep 3600"]
           tolerations:
           - key: "node.kubernetes.io/not-ready"
             operator: Exists
     EOF
   - Wait for DaemonSet pods to reach Running on new nodes (kubectl get ds/image-prepull -n kube-system)
5) Warm KV/Model cache priming (best-effort)
   - Kick off a small job that makes a few inference calls against each model variant to populate in-memory caches (or run a lightweight curl script against local node IPs).
   - Example Job: kubectl create job --from=cronjob/model-warmup model-warmup-manual -- image=warmup:latest --args='--models a,b,c --requests 100'
6) Verify readiness
   - Check node readiness: kubectl get nodes --selector=pool=warm-POOL -o wide
   - Pod eviction/throttles: kubectl describe nodes | grep -i pressure
   - Watch readiness probes on model pods (kubectl rollout status deployment/model-serving)
7) Route traffic / remove admission limits
   - If you had circuit-breaker/rate-limiter hooks to prevent new traffic, lift them during the warm window.
8) Tear down (for scheduled warmups)
   - After the event cools down, resize pool back or remove temporary Karpenter constraint patch. Document timeframe and reason in the scaling event ticket.

Rollbacks / aborts:
- If node provisioning is failing (nodes stuck in Provisioning/NotReady > 10m): cancel scaling and revert any provisioner changes; notify infra build team and escalate.
- If pre-pull DaemonSet causes unexpected image-pull storms on registry, scale it down immediately.

Cost evaluation quick formula:
- Extra-node-cost = n_extra * node_hourly_price * warm_hours
- Estimate savings: reduced request retries * avg_cost_per_retry + avoided SLA penalties.
- Track and log an event id for each warm action for later cost attribution.

Monitoring & SLOs to watch (example alerts):
- cluster_node_provisioning_latency > 120s (warning)
- image_pull_duration_seconds_bucket{le="30"} drop below baseline
- model_warm_hit_rate < 80% within 5m of traffic start (custom metric from model exporter)
- pod_start_time_p95 > baseline + 2s

Automation ideas (future work):
- Forecast-driven scheduler that auto-warms based on historical traffic patterns and calendar events.
- Light-weight "warm agent" DaemonSet that signals back to control plane when node-level caches are primed.
- Integrate with deployment rollouts: optionally pre-warm nodes that will run new model version prior to traffic switch.

Open questions / risks:
- Registry rate limits: pre-pulls can spike registry usage and hit quotas. Need throttles and pre-pull backoffs.
- Cost vs latency tradeoffs: too many static warm nodes wastes GPU hours; need strict tagging/billing for warm events.
- Compatibility with Dedicated pools (reserved capacity) vs autoscaler-driven pools.

Runbook post-action capture (minimum):
- Who initiated warm (name + ticket)
- Start / end timestamps of warm period
- Nodes added (instance ids) and AZs targeted
- Validation checks done (image pull checks, readiness, warm-hit-rate)
- Cost estimate for warm period and actual cost tagging
- Lessons learned / followups (create JIRA for infra changes)

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Add example Terraform snippets for managed node group scaling
- Bake a small warm-image that pre-populates disk with base model weights to shorten disk IO time
- Prototype a model-warm-hit exporter (Prometheus) that reports per-node primed status

Appendix: useful commands
- List nodes in warm pool: kubectl get nodes -l node-pool=warm-POOL -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'
- Check image pull logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system daemonset/image-prepull -f
- Resize (GKE): gcloud container clusters resize CLUSTER --node-pool POOL --num-nodes TARGET --zone ZONE
- Resize (EKS): eksctl scale nodegroup --cluster CLUSTER --name POOL --nodes TARGET

If you're executing this runbook for a customer-facing event, please ping #sre-deploy and @oncall-sre on Slack and attach the ticket link.

End of draft.

---
Editors: Priya (priority thresholds), Ethan (automation ideas), Lina (cost tagging)
